A statute is a written law formally created and enacted by a legislative body — such as a parliament, a congress, or a state or national assembly. It is the most official, deliberate, and explicit form of law in existence: one that didn't emerge from custom, tradition, or a judge's decision, but was specifically drafted in writing, debated, voted on, and officially approved by elected (or appointed) lawmakers.

If you imagine law as a family of rules, a statute is the most direct member of that family — the one where society, through its representatives, sat down and said: "This is the rule. It is written. It is official. Everyone must follow it."
Who Creates Statutes?

Statutes are created exclusively by legislatures — the bodies of people whose specific job is to make laws. Examples include:

The U.S. Congress at the federal level, state legislatures within each American state, the UK Parliament, the Indian Parliament, and so on. Every country and most sub-national regions (states, provinces) have their own legislative body, and each can produce statutes within their area of authority.

Crucially, a statute cannot be created by a single person acting alone — not even a president or a prime minister. It requires a formal group process: drafting, debating, voting, and finally approval (often by an executive, like a president signing a bill).
How a Statute Comes Into Existence

A statute begins its life as a bill — a proposal for a law. The bill is introduced in the legislature, debated, sometimes amended, and then voted upon. If it passes, it is sent for final approval (in many systems, a president or monarch signs or "assents" to it). At that point, the bill officially becomes a statute — a binding law of the land.

This is an important distinction: a bill is a proposed statute; a statute is what a bill becomes once it is passed and enacted. Until it clears the full process, it has no legal force. The word "enact" (meaning to formally put into effect) is closely associated with statutes — you will often see phrases like "the legislature enacted a statute" or "the statute was enacted in 1990."
What Statutes Cover

Statutes can govern virtually any area of human life and society. A legislature can write a statute about anything it has the authority to regulate. Common examples include:

Criminal law — statutes define what counts as a crime (theft, assault, fraud) and prescribe punishments. Tax law — statutes determine what and how much people and businesses must pay in taxes. Civil rights — statutes can prohibit discrimination based on race, gender, religion, and so on. Traffic law — statutes set speed limits, licensing requirements, and road rules. Contract and business law — statutes regulate how contracts work, how companies can be formed, and how commerce is conducted. Environmental law — statutes can mandate pollution limits and protect natural resources.

The breadth is enormous. If a government body has jurisdiction over something, it can potentially write a statute about it.
Key Characteristics of a Statute

It is always written. This is non-negotiable. An unwritten rule, no matter how widely followed, is not a statute. Statutes exist in text — they are recorded, published, and accessible.

It is general and prospective. Statutes typically apply to all people (or a defined category of people) going forward from the date they take effect. They are not usually written to punish a specific individual retroactively for something already done (in fact, many legal systems prohibit such "ex post facto" laws).

It is binding. Once enacted, a statute is not optional. People and institutions within its jurisdiction must comply with it. Violating a statute can result in penalties — fines, imprisonment, lawsuits, or other legal consequences, depending on the nature of the statute.

It can be repealed or amended. Because a statute is created by a legislature, the same (or a later) legislature can vote to change or eliminate it. A statute is not permanent by nature — it remains in force until it is officially repealed (cancelled) or amended (modified).

It must comply with a higher authority. In countries with a constitution, statutes cannot violate constitutional principles. If a court finds that a statute conflicts with the constitution, it can strike it down and declare it invalid. This is what happens during landmark constitutional court cases.
How Statutes Differ from Other Types of Law

Understanding statute becomes much richer when you see it alongside the other forms that law can take.

Statute vs. Common Law (Case Law): Common law is law that develops through the decisions judges make in court cases over time. When a judge decides a case in a novel way, that decision can serve as a precedent — a guide for how future courts should rule in similar situations. This body of judge-made law is called common law. It was never voted on by any legislature; it evolved through court practice, often over centuries. A statute, by contrast, is deliberately crafted by lawmakers. In most modern legal systems, when a statute and common law conflict, the statute wins — written law overrides judge-made law. One of the historic functions of legislatures has been to write statutes to clarify, reform, or override common law rules they considered outdated or unjust.

Statute vs. Regulation: A regulation (also called a "rule" in some contexts) is made not by the legislature but by an executive or administrative agency — for example, an environmental protection agency or a tax authority. However, agencies can only make regulations because a statute authorizes them to do so. The legislature passes a statute that says "Agency X is empowered to create detailed rules about Topic Y." The resulting rules are regulations, not statutes. Regulations are meant to fill in technical details that a legislature cannot or does not wish to specify in the statute itself. So the statute is the parent; the regulation is the child that operates within the boundaries the statute sets.

Statute vs. Constitution: A constitution is the supreme law in most countries — the foundational document that establishes the basic structure of government and protects fundamental rights. A statute sits below the constitution in the legal hierarchy. Every statute must be consistent with the constitution. If it isn't, courts can declare it unconstitutional and void. The constitution, unlike ordinary statutes, typically requires a much more difficult process (like a supermajority vote or a national referendum) to be changed.

Statute vs. Ordinance: An ordinance is a local law passed by a city council, county board, or similar local governing body. It functions like a statute at the local level — written, formally enacted, binding — but its authority is limited to the local jurisdiction. A statute passed by a national or state legislature has broader reach and generally supersedes an ordinance if they conflict.

Statute vs. Treaty: An international treaty is an agreement between countries. It is not passed by a single legislature in the same way, though many systems require a legislature to ratify (formally approve) treaties. The relationship between treaties and statutes varies by country.
Where Statutes Are Stored and Found

Because statutes accumulate over time, they are organized into collections called codes or compilations. For example, in the United States, federal statutes are organized into the United States Code (U.S.C.), which is divided into titles by subject matter (Title 26 is tax law, Title 18 is criminal law, and so on). Individual U.S. states have their own codes as well.

When lawyers and judges reference a statute, they typically cite it using its location in this code — for example, "42 U.S.C. § 1983" means Title 42 of the United States Code, Section 1983. The § symbol simply means "section."
The Phrase "Statute of Limitations"

This is one of the most widely encountered uses of the word "statute" in everyday life. A statute of limitations is a law (a statute) that sets a time limit on how long a person or government has to bring a legal case after an event occurs. Once that window closes, the right to sue or prosecute is typically gone forever, regardless of how strong the case might be.

For example, if a statute of limitations on personal injury lawsuits is three years, and you were injured in an accident, you must file your lawsuit within three years or lose the legal right to do so. The rationale is fairness and practicality: memories fade, evidence disappears, and people deserve to move on with their lives without the indefinite threat of legal action.
The Adjective: Statutory

When you see the word statutory, it simply means "relating to, created by, or required by a statute." Some examples:

Statutory rights are rights you have because a statute granted them to you — as opposed to rights that exist only because of a contract or a court decision. Statutory rape is a term for sexual activity that is criminalized by statute because one party is below the age of consent defined in that statute, regardless of whether consent was given. Statutory interpretation refers to the process courts use to figure out what a statute actually means — because statutes are written in words, and words can sometimes be ambiguous or unclear when applied to real situations judges didn't anticipate.
Statutory Interpretation — Why It Matters

No matter how carefully a legislature drafts a statute, the law will eventually be applied to situations its authors didn't foresee. When that happens, courts must interpret the statute — figure out what it means and how it should apply. This is a significant legal discipline in itself. Judges ask: What do the words literally say? What did the lawmakers intend? What interpretation best fits the statute's overall purpose? This is why court cases often turn not on disputed facts, but on disputed interpretations of what a statute means.
A Practical Summary

Think of a statute as society's formal, written instruction manual for a specific area of life, produced by the people's elected representatives through a structured, official process. It is more deliberate than custom, more democratic than a judge's ruling, more specific than a constitution, and more authoritative than a regulation. When you hear phrases like "the law says," or "it's against the law," there's a very good chance a statute is what's being referred to. Statutes are the backbone of a modern legal system — the clearest expression of a society's collective decisions about the rules everyone must live by.
